slides.headline: The Conditional Activation Model
slides.subhead: Uncovering Policy Demand Responses to AI-Driven Automation
slides.notes: Open with the aggregate puzzle: why do information experiments on automation risk so often produce null or conflicting effects? The CAM framework treats this as a composition effect across two gates.

blocks.label: Author
blocks.text: Ignacio Urbina · Stony Brook University · April 2026

slides.headline: Automation exposure is widespread, yet experimental evidence on policy demand remains inconclusive.
slides.subhead: Frey & Osborne (2017) estimate 47% of U.S. occupations face high automation risk. Public awareness is high (Pew 2023), but experiments linking risk information to policy preferences yield mixed results.
slides.notes: Frame as a scientific puzzle. The disconnect between public awareness and experimental null effects is what motivates the paper.

items.title: Structural labor market shift
items.detail: Routine cognitive and manual tasks face increasing automation pressure

items.title: Policy demand channel
items.detail: Standard models predict risk exposure → demand for retraining, regulation, redistribution

items.title: Empirical gap
items.detail: Experimental tests of this channel produce inconsistent or null aggregate effects

items.detail: of U.S. employment (Frey & Osborne 2017)

items.label: Public concern
items.detail: major concern about AI workforce impact (Pew 2023)

slides.headline: Three traditions converge: personal risk information should increase policy demand.
slides.subhead: Self-interest theory, threat-motivated cognition, and egotropic economic voting each predict that learning one's occupation faces automation risk should increase support for protective policies.
slides.notes: Self-interest: Meltzer & Richard (1981). Threat motivation: Albertson & Gadarian (2015). Egotropic: Kinder & Kiewiet (1981).

items.label: Self-interest
items.detail: Workers facing losses seek compensatory policy (Meltzer & Richard 1981)

items.label: Threat-motivated cognition
items.detail: Threat perception focuses attention on protection (Albertson & Gadarian 2015)

items.label: Egotropic voting
items.detail: Individual economic exposure drives policy demand (Kinder & Kiewiet 1981)

slides.headline: Experimental results are inconsistent: null, positive, and opposing effects coexist.
slides.subhead: Studies examining conditional effects find heterogeneity that washes out in the aggregate.
slides.notes: The pivot comes from Arntz et al. (2024), who find opposing subgroup effects that cancel at the aggregate level. Wu (2022) and Im (2023) provide further evidence for conditional moderation by ideology, education, and prior beliefs.

items.title: Null aggregate effects are common
items.detail: Zhang & Hou (2022), Magistro et al. (2024): personalized risk information → null ATE on policy preferences

items.title: Positive findings exist but with different designs
items.detail: Gallego et al. (2022): distinct treatment and sample yield positive effects

items.title: Subgroup heterogeneity drives cancellation
items.detail: Arntz et al. (2024): opposing subgroup effects cancel in the aggregate. Wu (2022), Im (2023): effects moderated by ideology, education, prior beliefs

slides.headline: The unconditional ATE averages over heterogeneous subgroups — the estimand is misspecified.
slides.subhead: Weak aggregate effects may reflect composition rather than preference stability. The relevant estimand conditions on who absorbs the signal and on who is personally exposed.
slides.notes: Pivotal slide. Reframe from ATE to CATE. Note that in this study the aggregate effect is not itself null — it is positive but modest, and it understates the group that actually moves.

left.label: Standard estimand
left.text: E[Y(1) − Y(0)]: unconditional ATE across the full sample

right.label: Proposed estimand
right.text: E[Y(1) − Y(0) | trust stratum, anxiety × automation risk]: CATE by expert-trust stratum and by joint exposure

slides.headline: Two sequential gates: expert trust, then joint activation (anxiety × automation risk).
slides.subhead: Trust governs whether the expert signal is absorbed at all. Activation requires dispositional vigilance and personal exposure together, not either alone.
slides.notes: Gate 1 is about absorption, not agreement: a respondent who discounts the source has nothing to update on. Gate 2 is conjunctive by construction — the prediction is a corner, not two main effects.

items.title: Gate 1: expert trust
items.detail: Whether the signal is absorbed at all. Recovered as a principal stratum from pre-treatment covariates, not a raw post-treatment split

items.title: Gate 2: joint requirement
items.detail: Neither trait anxiety nor own-occupation automation risk alone should be sufficient to move policy demand

items.title: Below-threshold pathway
items.detail: Beliefs update without policy preference change (cool cognition)

slides.headline: The two-gate structure predicts three qualitatively distinct cognitive pathways.
slides.subhead: Each pathway corresponds to a different exit point in the information-processing sequence. A weak population-level ATE is the expected signature when the three pathways are mixed.
slides.notes: This is a theoretical slide — no empirical numbers yet. The three pathways are derived from the gate structure, not from data. The key theoretical claim is that weak aggregates are predicted by the model under heterogeneous mixing, not anomalous.

items.label: 1. Signal discounted
items.detail: The expert estimate is not absorbed; no downstream processing regardless of anxiety or personal exposure

items.label: 2. Cool cognition
items.detail: The signal is absorbed and beliefs update, but exposure is insufficient to initiate policy search

items.label: 3. Activated persuasion
items.detail: Both gates cleared; sustained elaboration of threat translates into demand for protective policy

blocks.label: Prediction
blocks.text: If the three pathways are mixed in the population, the unconditional ATE will understate the responsive subgroup — producing the weak or null aggregate effects observed in prior work.

slides.headline: Pre-registered between-subjects experiment, N = 901 U.S. workers.
slides.subhead: Three-step belief correction protocol with individualized treatment intensity. 475 treated, 426 control.
slides.notes: Workers compress beliefs toward the middle of the scale regardless of actual risk, so the expert estimate lands as a genuine informational shock for most respondents.

items: Reveal expert estimate; display belief gap

left.label: Design property
left.text: Both moderators are measured before treatment, so the activation corner is a fixed partition of pre-treatment characteristics rather than an outcome of the manipulation.

items.title: Outcome
items.detail: Policy demand index: 5 items, 7-pt scale (ω = 0.83)

items.title: Expert trust
items.detail: 5-point item, post-treatment only

items.title: Automation risk
items.detail: Own-occupation percentile, pre-treatment

items.title: Trait anxiety
items.detail: 4-item scale, pre-treatment (ω = 0.92)

slides.headline: A five-item policy demand index and three moderators operationalize the two-gate structure.
slides.subhead: Policy demand is scored by a graded response model. Trust is post-treatment; anxiety and automation risk are pre-treatment.
slides.notes: The battery deliberately spans redistribution, regulation, retraining, labor protections, and employment limits to avoid anchoring to a single ideological frame. Trust is a single post-treatment item — a limitation, but necessary to avoid contaminating control. Automation risk is the expert percentile for the respondent's own occupation, so it is fixed before the experiment.

cells: 5 items, 7-pt scale (ω = 0.83), scored by a graded response model (EAP)
Single 5-pt item, post-treatment, treated arm only

blocks.label: Asymmetry
blocks.text: Trust is observed only in the treated arm; anxiety and automation risk are observed in both. Carrying trust into the control arm is the identification problem the next slide solves.

slides.headline: The treatment landed: respondents understood it, were surprised by it, and updated on it.
slides.subhead: 93.5% pass the factual check. Mean belief gap = 2.44 (SD = 36.1), range [−83, +94].
slides.notes: The gap is wide in both directions, so the treatment is not a one-sided alarm: roughly as many respondents learn their risk is lower than they thought as higher. Self-reported belief updating tracks the size of the gap (Spearman ρ = 0.66), which is what makes it a genuine informational shock rather than a confirmation exercise.

items.label: Factual check
items.detail: passed the expert-methodology check

items.label: Updating × gap
items.detail: larger gaps produce larger self-reported belief updating

slides.headline: Trust is measured only in the treated arm; a pre-treatment proxy carries it into both.
slides.subhead: Random forest proxy → principal score → Hájek weighting of both arms. Identified by randomization plus principal ignorability.
slides.notes: Emphasize that nothing post-treatment enters the weights. The proxy is built only from covariates fixed before randomization, which is exactly why the same weights can be applied in the control arm. The assumption is principal ignorability, and it is untestable in this design — the next slide reports how badly it would have to fail.

steps.title: Proxy
steps.detail: Random forest on 15 pre-treatment terms predicts the 5-pt trust rating

steps.title: Principal score
steps.detail: Logit of Truster (trust ≥ 4) on the proxy gives pᵢ for every respondent

steps.title: Contrast
steps.detail: Hájek-weighted arm means: pᵢ for Trusters, 1 − pᵢ for mid/low

left.label: Identifying assumption
left.text: \[ \tau_{\text{Truster}} = E[\eta(1) - \eta(0) \mid \text{Truster}] \] Identified under randomization plus principal ignorability: pᵢ is a function of pre-treatment covariates only, so the same weights apply in both arms.

slides.headline: The unconditional effect is positive and stable across covariate sets (0.22–0.28 SD).
slides.subhead: Policy demand η, standardized. Every specification excludes zero; adjustment moves the point estimate by less than 0.07.
slides.notes: This is the starting point, and it is deliberately unremarkable: a real but modest aggregate effect. The rest of the talk asks who it belongs to. Estimates are OLS with HC1 standard errors.

slides.headline: Trust gates absorption: the Truster effect is roughly three times the mid/low one.
slides.subhead: Hájek principal-score weighting of both arms. Bootstrap B = 2000, with the proxy, the logit and the weights refit in every replicate.
slides.notes: The contrast is the quantity the theory predicts, and it is positive with P(>0) = 0.99 — but it is also the underpowered one, which the power slide addresses directly. Covariate-adjusted estimates attenuate slightly and preserve the ordering.

items.title: Covariate-adjusted (FWL)
items.detail: 0.329 / 0.110 / 0.219 — same ordering, modestly attenuated

blocks.label: How badly would principal ignorability have to fail?
blocks.text: Driving these estimates to zero requires a hidden differential treatment response of −1.17 SD for the Truster CATE and −0.52 SD for the contrast: large, and opposite in sign to the mechanism under study.

slides.headline: Among Trusters, the effect concentrates in the high-anxiety × high-risk corner.
slides.subhead: A fixed top-tercile rule on both pre-treatment moderators, with no cutoff or sharpness parameter estimated. 105 of 901 respondents (11.7%) qualify.
slides.notes: Stress that nothing here is fitted except the treatment effect itself: corner membership is a deterministic function of two pre-treatment variables. The two moderators are near-independent (corr = 0.014), so the corner is not just a restatement of one of them. Mid/low trust shows no corner, which is the pattern the two-gate structure predicts.

items.title: A fixed rule, nothing fitted
items.detail: Top tercile of trait anxiety (z ≥ 0.53) AND of own automation risk (≥ 54.5th percentile), both pre-treatment

items.title: The moderators are near-independent
items.detail: corr(A, R) = 0.014; the 11.7% corner share matches the ≈ 11.1% implied by independent terciles

items.title: Corner effect is 2.4× the outside effect
items.detail: 0.685 in the corner vs 0.288 outside it, among Trusters

items.title: The cutoff choice does not drive it
items.detail: δ's 95% CI excludes zero at the median, the 58.3rd percentile and the tercile

blocks.label: No corner without the first gate
blocks.text: For mid/low trust the corner increment is null: δ = 0.194 [−0.056, 0.466]. The conjunction only pays off for respondents who absorbed the signal.

slides.headline: Two of the four headline quantities are well powered; the other two are not.
slides.subhead: Minimum detectable effect at 80% power, computed from the same bootstrap standard errors the estimates use.
slides.notes: The point of putting this in the main talk rather than an appendix: a null or marginal estimate is ambiguous between 'no effect' and 'too small for this design to see' unless power is addressed directly. The stratum contrast and the corner increments fall below their own MDEs, so their significance should not be read as evidence the design was well powered to detect them.

items.label: Truster CATE
items.detail: power at the observed effect; MDE 0.28

items.label: Truster corner effect
items.detail: clears its own MDE of 0.44

items.label: Stratum contrast
items.detail: observed effect sits below its MDE of 0.33

items.label: Mid/low corner increment
items.detail: far below its MDE of 0.36

blocks.label: What this licenses
blocks.text: The Truster results are the ones this design can carry. A null on the mid/low corner increment cannot distinguish a genuinely absent effect from a real one the study lacks the power to see.

slides.headline: Aggregate effects understate the subgroup that responds.
slides.subhead: The two-gate architecture generalizes to any persuasion domain with expert sources and dispositional moderators.
slides.notes: Scope: U.S. online workers, liberal skew, single post-treatment trust item, immediate measurement, Frey & Osborne 2017 risk estimates. The trust result is identified under principal ignorability, which is untestable here; a design measuring trust before treatment would resolve it directly. Generalization domains: climate, vaccines, trade.

items: Theoretical: a two-gate model accounts for conflicting prior results as composition across pathways rather than as preference stability.

Methodological: trust is post-treatment and observed in the treated arm only; a pre-treatment proxy plus principal-score weighting recovers stratum effects from both arms under an explicit, sensitivity-tested assumption.
Empirical: the Truster effect (0.40 SD) is about three times the mid/low one, and among Trusters the high-anxiety × high-risk corner reaches 0.69 SD, roughly 2.4× the effect outside it.
Implication: risk communication that ignores who trusts the source, and who is personally exposed, will understate responsiveness in exactly the group that responds.

right.label: Scope
right.text: N = 901 U.S. workers · 62% Democratic including leaners · immediate measurement · trust identified under principal ignorability. Generalizes to climate, vaccines, trade.
